New aspects of C2 selectivity in electrochemical CO2 reduction over oxide-derived copper Aamir Hassan Shah,a,b Yanjie Wang,*a,b Sajjad Hussain,a,b Muhammad Bilal Akbar,a,b Abebe Reda Woldu,a,b Xuehua Zhanga,b and Tao He*a,b
The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to yield C2 products is of particular interest in solar-to-fuel conversion schemes. The nanocrystalline oxide derived copper (ODCu) electrodes are specifically attractive due to their high Faradic efficiency towards C2 hydrocarbons like ethylene, ethane, acetate and ethanol. However, the mechanistic understanding of this special selectivity is still an impediment. In this work, ODCu is obtained from Cu2O nanowires and employed for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction, during which ethylene is found to be the major product with Faradic efficiency of 65% at 0.8 V (vs RHE). By in-situ photoresponse measurement, combined with the ex situ structure and composition analysis, Cu2O is demonstrated to be persistent on the surface of ODCu throughout the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) even at high applied bias (1.0 V vs RHE), while Cu2O is not present on the bulk Cu foil. Density functional theory calculations are employed to further investigate the correlation between the surface Cu2O on ODCu and its C2 selectivity performance, which is attributed to the orbital interactions between the persistent oxide and CO2 reduction intermediates. Noted that uncovering the active sites is the initial step to understand the surface reaction chemistry in CO2RR, here we propose that the presence of Cu2O is the key for C2 selectivity during CO2RR in ODCu system, which may facilitate the development of highly efficient catalysts.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
One challenge mankind facing now is to attenuate the critical issue of global warming by developing technologies to capture and convert carbon dioxide (CO2) — a greenhouse gas released mainly by burning of fossil fuels — to useful hydrocarbons. The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is promising as a viable CO2 utilization approach since it can occur under ambient conditions. Various transition metal catalysts have been used for CO2RR because of their available versatile dorbital electron states that participate in adsorption and/or facilitate the hydrocarbon formation, such as Cu, Au and Ag.1-3 C2 products like ethylene (C2H4) and ethanol (C2H5OH) are especially required, as they are widely used as chemical feedstock.4-6 Moreover, C2 products are more preferable than C1 due to their high energy density and the complicated industrial synthesis of C2 as compared to C1.7-9 Among various metal catalysts, Cu is unique owing to its ability to reduce CO2 to a significant amount of C2 and C3 hydrocarbons under ambient conditions. It is reported that bulk Cu usually favors the generation of methane (CH4) with a parasitic hydrogen evolution, while nanostructured Cu facilitates C2H4 production. Therefore, considerable efforts have been devoted to tune the structure of Cu, like Cu mesocrystals,10 Cu-halide confined mesh,11 Cu nanoparticles,12 and Cu nanowire.13 Specifically, it is reported that the Cu derived from reduction of thermally oxidized Cu or electrodeposited copper oxide exhibits efficient and selective CO2 reduction to C2 products at low overpotentials.14-17 The oxide derived copper (ODCu) was firstly utilized by Karl W. Frese for electrochemical reduction of CO2.18 Kanan and co-workers reported that ODCu exhibits high Faradic efficiencies and low overpotential for CO reduction.19 Furthermore, many groups have reported that it exhibits high selectivity performance for reducing CO2 to C2 products.
However, the origin of the enhanced activity for this ODCu catalyst is difficult to recognize, due to the complexity of CO2 reduction process and change in Cu states. To date, many factors have been proposed as the origin for the special performance of ODCu, such as high grain boundary density,1921 local pH,22-26 presence of sub-surface oxygen atoms,27-30 low coordinated atoms due to nanostructuring, crystal facets and crystallite size.31-36 Specifically, there is a controversy on the active sites in the Cu catalyst. Although metallic Cu is regarded as the only active species during the CO2RR in many reports,37,38 other researchers have reported the presence of a thin metastable Cu2O oxide layer during the CO2RR.5,39-43 The Cu+ present in the ODCu electrode surface can provide the adsorption sites for negatively charged CO2RR intermediates, leading to a higher C2 selectivity on these electrodes.5,39-42 Despite these results, the catalytic role of ODCu and sub-

surface oxygen is currently a controversial topic and needs further elucidation.38 In some reports the role of Cu2O on C2 selectivity is explained on the basis of positive charge of Cu+, which can adsorb CO2RR intermediates via electrostatic forces on its surface and, hence, relatively strong adsorption leads to better C2 selectivity. However, the role of negatively charged electrode surface under the influence of applied negative potential during the reaction is not considered, albeit several reports that ponder the influence of metastable oxide layer and thus the presence of Cu+ on C2 selectivity is considered.5,39-42 It is of utmost importance to understand the fundamental adsorption behavior of CO2 reduction intermediates on the electrode surface under the negative bias before implementing any technical consideration for this special C2 selective system. Even though the operando evidence has already been reported, the cost effectiveness and low detection limit still remain the issue.14,44 Moreover, rapid formation of native oxide on the metallic Cu surface without being applied a bias during the removal from reactor and exposure to air for ex situ analysis may complicate the evidence.14 Nevertheless, it is necessary to study the catalytic role of ODCu and the mechanism underlying its C2 selectivity performance in CO2RR, will facilitate the mechanistic understanding and design of more efficient catalysts for CO2 reduction.
Herein, we have synthesized relatively stable, highly C2 selective ODCu from Cu2O nanowires (NWs) on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) substrate. In situ photoresponse technique, combined with structure and composition analysis, can provide direct evidence for the presence of Cu2O during electrocatalytic CO2RR in the electrolyte. Considering the influence of applied negative bias, we believe that the presence of positive charges owing to Cu+ on the ODCu cannot be the key factor that leads to intermediate adsorption on a negatively charged electrode surface. Here we propose the concept of orbital interactions between the Cu2O on ODCu and CO2RR intermediates, which leads to enhanced amount of intermediates adsorption on the ODCu electrode and, thereby, the C2 selectivity.

sections.heading: Electrode and electrolyte preparation
sections.text:
KHCO3 (99.999% metal basis) and KOH (99.999% metal basis) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Cu metal target (99.995%) was purchased from Alfa Aesar. KHCO3 electrolyte solutions with different concentrations for electrolysis were prepared with 18.2 MΩ Milli-Q water, followed by being purged with Ar (99.999%) for 30 min and then with CO2 (99.999%) for 60 min.
FTO coated glass substrates were cut into shards of 11 cm2, and then cleaned by being sonicated sequentially for 30 min in water, acetone, isopropyl alcohol and Milli-Q water, and finally dried with a stream of Ar. Cu was deposited onto the obtained FTO electrodes via DC sputtering with an average growth rate of 2.65 nm s1 using Alliance-Concept DP 650 system. Cu2O
NWs was synthesized by electrochemical anodization of Cu film by the method reported elsewhere.45 Briefly, single phase Cu2O NWs were obtained by annealing Cu(OH)2 NWs at 600 °C in Ar atmosphere that were prepared by anodic polarization of Cu thin film in 3 M KOH electrolyte.

sections.heading: Characterizations
sections.text:
Morphology of Cu2O NWs were observed with a Hitachi SU8200 scanning electron microscope (SEM). Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were collected using Bruker D8 diffractometer with CuK radiation (0.15406 nm) for structure and composition study. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (ESCALAB250Xi, ThermoFisher) was used to determine the chemical state of Cu. The structure and element distribution were studied by transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Tecnai G2 F20 U-TWIN, FEI, USA) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM, HAADF, MODEL 3000, Fischione Instruments, USA) with energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) detector.
In situ photoresponse electrochemical measurements were performed with Zahner IM6 potentiostat (Zahner Elektrik, Kronach, Germany). Working electrode was kept parallel to counter electrode (Pt foil) to ensure uniform potential distribution across the electrode surface. Ag/AgCl was used as reference electrode for all the experiments. Unless stated otherwise, the obtained potentials were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale using the equation of E(vs RHE) = 0.197 + 0.059pH + E(vs Ag/AgCl).

sections.heading: Catalytic performance
sections.text:
Electrocatalytic gaseous products were produced in a 220 mL airtight O-ring glass reactor system and were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC). The electrolyte was vacuumed three times before the reaction so as to remove the dissolved gases and then purged with Ar for 30 min. The solution was then saturated with CO2 for 60 min. The electrochemical CO2RR was performed at different applied voltages (0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9 and 1.0 V vs RHE) for 90 min using the potentiostat. The gaseous products (H2, CO and C2H4) were quantified by a GCMS spectrometer (SHIMADZU, GCMS-DP2020) equipped with a barrier discharge ionization detector (BID-2010 plus). High purity He gas was used as the carrier gas. The samples were taken out from the catholyte after electrolysis. 1H-NMR measurements were performed on a Bruker 400 MHz NMR spectrometer, using a presaturation sequence to suppress the water signal. The 250 L of sample solution was mixed with 10 L of 0.1 M N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) as internal solvent, and 240 L of D2O as locking solvent, followed by being transferred into the NMR tube for recording 1H-NMR spectra.
Density functional theory calculations
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations of Cu2O with different concentration of oxygen, as well as adsorption energy of OCCO on Cu2O (111) and Cu (111), was performed using Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP).46 Hybrid Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06)47 and generalized gradient approximation (GGA) in the scheme of Perdew-Burke-

sections.heading: Structure and morphology characteristics
sections.text:
Cu2O film was prepared by anodization of a Cu layer in 3 M KOH and it is found to be nanowires, as shown in Fig. 1a,1b. Both high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image (Fig. 1c) and X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) patterns (Fig. S1) correspond to crystalline Cu2O. After CO2RR there is barely change in the morphology (Fig. 1e,1f), while the XRD patterns indicate the formation of Cu (Fig. S1), as also evidenced by the HRTEM result (Fig. 1g). It is worth noting that there is a thin layer (several nanometers) of Cu2O on the surface of Cu in ODCu (Fig. 1g), indicating the possibility of the presence of Cu+ during CO2RR. EDX elemental mapping image have clearly implied distribution of Cu and O along the nanowire (Fig. 1d,1h). In spite of the inaccuracy of EDX for O element analysis, the noticeable bright red spots in Fig. 1h indicate the non-negligible amount of O element over the ODCu nanowire.
To gain more insight into the chemical state of Cu in ODCu, Cu2O NWs were held at at 1.0 V vs RHE in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 for 90 min and immediately their composition was analyzed ex situ using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (Fig. 2a). The spectrum of Cu2O is similar to that of Cu. The shoulder peaks separately located near the above two mains peaks and the satellite peaks at around 944.5 and 963.5 eV demonstrates the presence of Cu2+, which is probably due to the oxidation upon exposure to air. The major peaks located at 932.6 and 952.4 eV correspond to Cu 2p2/3 and Cu 2p1/2 of Cu0 or Cu+, respectively, which cannot be distinguished due to the small binding energy difference (0.1 eV). Accordingly, Auger electron spectroscopy of Cu LMM signal is obtained so as to
discriminate the oxidation state of Cu0 and Cu+, (Fig. 2b), showing that the surface characteristic of ODCu is similar to Cu2O NWs, mainly consisting of Cu+ (Cu2O) state at 570.1 eV and there is also a small peak at 568.1 eV corresponding to Cu0 on ODCu. Since XPS is a surface sensitive technique for several nanometers of top layer on the sample, this indicates that, under CO2RR working conditions, the top several nanometers of Cu2O remains there, even though the bulk Cu2O NWs are reduced to Cu by the negative bias.
Persistent presence of Cu2O in the ODCu electrode
To further confirm the persistent presence of Cu2O in the ODCu electrodes, in situ characterizations under the working conditions are necessary. Therefore, in situ photoresponse measurements of the Cu2O electrodes were carried out in CO2saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte under different bias voltages. Once the sample was taken out from the electrolyte, specifically, this can avoid ambiguity of instantaneous reformation of surface oxides in air after removing the applied negative bias.14

Fig. 3 In situ photoresponse with polarization of Cu2O electrode at (a) 0.5 and (b) 1.0 V, and of Cu foil at (c) 1.0 V vs RHE in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 (pH 6.8) under chopping white-light illumination.
Initially, the reduction current density rapidly decreases under the applied negative bias voltages due to reduction of Cu2O to metallic Cu, and then a relatively stable current value is achieved (Fig. 3a,3b). Interestingly, however, the current density increases sharply once white light is shed onto the electrode even still under the applied negative bias (Insets of Fig. 3a,3b), indicating the ODCu electrode is photoresponsive, which can be repeatedly observed even after 90-min cathodic polarization. Hence, under working conditions there are either CuO or Cu2O in ODCu. Since the negative potential acts as electron source to ‘scavenge’ the photogenerated holes, the chance of photocorrosion of Cu2O to CuO by holes is minimal, indicating that only Cu2O is present and the Cu2+ observed in XPS analysis is from air exposure. In addition, no such photoresponse is observed when Cu foil is illuminated with the
same light intensity (Fig. 3c). Combined with the HRTEM and XPS analysis, we propose
that Cu2O is always present in the ODCu electrode during the CO2RR. Definitely, this is not simply due to surface oxidation induced by exposure to air or re-formation of oxide in the absence of applied bias. The presence of such persistent oxide layer agrees well with previous report that no complete Cu2O reduction occurs and a metastable oxide layer of Cu2O still exists on the electrode surface even after a long-time cathodic polarization.5,50 These findings challenge the conventional claim about the presence of only active metallic Cu (Cu0) during the CO2RR and, thereby, implying the possible role of Cu2O in the unique catalysis selectivity of ODCu.
Influence from persistent Cu2O and applied potential on CO2RR selectivity
The CO2RR activity of ODCu is further studied under a series applied potentials without illumination. Fig. S2 shows the corresponding chronoamperometry curves, in which the initial reduction peaks for Cu+ to Cu0 are observed and thereafter more negative bias leads to higher steady state current density. The CO2 reduction products are measured by analyzing gaseous products after 90-min electrolysis in CO2saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Fig. 4). Only three gaseous products (H2, CO and C2H4) are observed; and no any liquid products can be detected in terms of 1HNMR analysis, except trace amount of formate (Fig. S3). It is noted that negligible amount of ethane is observed at 0.8 V, which is otherwise absent at all other applied potentials.

It is found that the dominant product at all applied potentials is C2H4 with the maximum Faradic efficiency (FE) value of 65% at 0.8 V, which is proposed to be resulted from the balance of intermediate dimerization and desorption under different bias voltages. The FE of C2H4 first increases steadily when the potential becomes more negative until 0.8 V (Fig. 4a) because the dimerization of intermediates is more facile at the surface anchoring sites than the charge transfer to form other hydrocarbons;51 while it starts to decrease when the potential becomes further more negative as the surface bound intermediates are more likely to be desorbed at more negative potentials. We are aware of the fact that our results are exceptional in the case that barely detectable formate or ethanol is observed, which is otherwise reported on Cu and ODCu electrodes surfaces. The alteration in selectivity only towards CO and C2H4 in our case may be due to the availability and relative higher stability of Cu+ sites (during the CO2 reduction experiment) in their initial state. Another explanation for this effect may be due to the enhanced CO2 reduction on defect sites present in the ODCu surface. It is noted that, at a less negative bias, the second major product is CO. The FE of CO increases when the potential increases from 0.5 to 0.6 V, and then it starts to decrease with increase in the potential. Such trend is determined by many factors, including CO adsorption, further reduction to C2H4, and competition with HER.
Since the FE is an important factor to evaluate the CO2RR selectivity and the total current density varies significantly with the changes in applied bias voltage, the partial current density for each product obtained by multiplying the total current density with FE is plotted in Fig. 4b. The reaction rate can thus be analyzed in terms of partial current density. For example, the FE of CO and C2H4 starts to decrease after 0.6 and 0.8 V, respectively; while the partial current density for all the products demonstrates a trend of increment with more negative bias, but H2 is the fastest. This suggest that such a decrease in the FE of CO and C2H4 may be because of more rapidly increased reaction rate of H2 (Fig. 4b).
Based on the above product analysis from CO2 reduction on ODCu, the mechanism is proposed here. It is reported that
local pH of the ODCu electrode surface has a great impact on the C2 selectivity of CO2RR,50,52 as the increased rate of catalytic reactions on a roughened surface can elevate the local pH, resulting in reduced CO2 protonation dependence on the pH value. Meanwhile, the pH independent reaction route via CO dimerization is not affected. Consequently, the CH4 formation is decreased and C2H4 production is enhanced.53-55 However, it is reported previously that the onset potential of C2H4 formation shifts to a less negative value (i.e., lower overpotential) in this case, which cannot only be attributed to a higher local pH, but also partly to the promoted stability of Cu2O at a higher local pH.5 Obviously, various CO2RR results in different KHCO3 solutions are good evidence for this (Fig. 5). It is already stated that, owing to the buffer capacity difference, higher KHCO3 concentration results in higher bulk pH but leads to lower local pH adjacent to the electrode surface.24 Clearly, the C2H4 production drops with decrease in the local pH by increasing the electrolyte concentration, meanwhile H2 production increases; which is due to the above mentioned low pH dependent C2H4 formation, as well as Cu2O stabilization.

sections.heading: C2 selectivity studied by density functional theory calculations
sections.text:
The mechanism underlying the C2 selectivity performance of ODCu is further studied by the density functional theory (DFT) simulations. The *OCCO is produced by dimerization of *CO during the CO2RR and is proposed to be a key intermediate for C2 products such as ethylene, where * resembles the adsorption state. Since the adsorbed intermediates and their respective stability can influence the products and, thereby, the reaction selectivity, analyzing the adsorption energy of OCCO on Cu2O from that on Cu is crucial to understand the mechanism underlying the C2 selectivity. Considering both the dominant surface of Cu2O and ODCu is (111) (Fig. S1), the adsorption energy of OCCO intermediate on Cu(111) and Cu2O(111) surfaces is calculated respectively to compare the stability of OCCO intermediate on these facets. Bridge adsorption configuration of OCCO is employed on these surfaces, where the O and C atoms of OCCO are bound as a bridge with Cu atoms of Cu(111) and Cu2O(111) slabs. The optimized structures are shown in Fig. 6. The calculated total energies of different systems are listed in Table S1, from which it can be calculated that the adsorption energy of OCCO on Cu(111) and Cu2O(111) is 3.20 and 5.49 eV, respectively. The more negative adsorption energy of OCCO intermediate on Cu2O(111) surface indicates that *OCCO is energetically more stable on Cu2O (111). Thus, the presence of a thin-layer metastable Cu2O in ODCu can play a significant role in stabilizing the CO2RR intermediates and, accordingly, in the C2 selectivity.
In addition, DFT simulation is also used to study the correlation between the solid surface and its performance of intermediate stabilization by considering the orbital interactions. It is found that the valence band of Cu2Ox with all oxygen contents is largely contributed by the O 2p and Cu 3d states, as well as a small contribution of s and p orbitals of Cu and s orbital of O (Fig. S5). The contribution of these states increases with increment in the oxygen content. Furthermore, Fig. 7 reveals that the p electrons of O and d electrons of Cu tend to be delocalized into deep energy levels with increasing oxygen content in the electrode. Such enhanced orbital delocalization can lead to large hybridization between CO2RR intermediates and ODCu electrode and, thereby, facilitate the adsorption of CO2RR intermediates, which is similar to the previous report that the p-orbital delocalization of Bi catalyst can facilitate the intermediate adsorption and, thus, boost the CO2RR rate to formate.56

Therefore, in the ODCu electrodes, the presence of p orbitals of O plays an important role in the adsorption of CO2RR intermediates. The CO2RR pathways can be changed greatly with and without such p orbitals of O in the valence band maximum, or in other words, with and without the presence of metastable Cu2O in the electrodes. As indicated above, only two products of C2H4 and CO are observed via CO2RR under the given range of applied potentials (i.e., 0.5 ~ 1.0 V), with C2H4 as the major product. Compared to pure Cu electrode, the relatively strong adsorption of the CO2RR intermediates like OCCO on the ODCu electrode due to the persistent Cu2O (even with trace amount) is in favor of the formation of C2H4. Moreover, the applied negative potentials may facilitate the orbital delocalization of the p electrons of O and d electrons of Cu and, thus, in favor of the hybridization between CO2RR intermediates and ODCu electrode. Accordingly, the adsorption of CO2RR intermediates can be improved, resulting in higher selectivity of C2H4 production. Further study is expected to confirm this hypothesis.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: In summary, we have successfully synthesized the Cu2O NWs on FTO glass and performed the electrolysis in CO2-saturated KHCO3 electrolyte solutions. Here we present direct evidence about the presence of Cu2O using in situ photoresponse and ex situ measurements of HRTEM and XPS. We have also explained the role of ODCu in the C2 product selectivity in terms of the intermediate stabilization due to orbital interactions between the persistent Cu2O on ODCu, as well as CO2RR intermediates and influence of the applied negative potential. We envision that these findings can provide better understanding on the behavior of ODCu electrodes and facilitate R&D of the selective catalysts for CO2 reduction.
